items.title: What's new in Pyroscope: profile more of your workflows, troubleshoot with AI agents, and more
items.summary: When an application slows down or memory usage keeps climbing, knowing which code is responsible can help you find a fix faster. Continuous profiling gives you that visibility, so you can see where your application spends resources such as CPU time and memory.We’ve made updates to Pyroscope, our open source continuous profiling database, that make it easier to profile your applications, find performance bottlenecks, and optimize your code, whether you're doing the work yourself or with an AI agent. Highlights include:Profile more of your workloads: Memory profiling for Python and Rust, and .NET support on Windows, helps you find performance bottlenecks across more of your services.Let AI agents work with your profiling data: Pyroscope commands in gcx, the Grafana CLI, let an agent query your profiles directly.See more of your profiling data in Grafana: Exemplars and a new Call Tree view help you explore your profiles visually, whether you're investigating on your own or looking at what an agent found.Many of these capabilities build directly on Pyroscope 2.0, the ground-up rearchitecture of Pyroscope that makes continuous profiling more cost-effective at scale (in our production environment, it reduced the symbol storage footprint by up to 95%). For example, exemplars require the v2 storage layer that Pyroscope 2.0 is built on. Read on to learn more about some of the latest updates. And for a full list of recent changes, see the release notes for Pyroscope and Profiles Drilldown.Profile more of your workloadsMemory profiling and Windows support have been some of the most frequently requested features for Pyroscope. If you run Python or Rust services, you can now use the Pyroscope SDKs to see where their memory goes, not just their CPU time. If you run .NET applications on Windows, you can now profile those, too.Find memory leaks and heavy allocation: memory profiling for PythonMemory issues can be hard to track down from metrics alone. A container's memory graph shows that usage is climbing, but not which code is allocating that memory. CPU profiles don't answer that either, since they show where your code spends time. Memory profiles show which code paths allocate the most memory and which allocated the memory that's still in use, which is what you need when a service's memory keeps growing, or its allocations drive up garbage collection work.The Python SDK now supports memory profiling, so you can see which code allocates the most memory and which code allocated the memory that's still in use, alongside the CPU profiles you already collect. Enable it with mem_enabled=True:pyroscope.configure(    application_name = "my.python.app",    server_address   = "http://my-pyroscope-server:4040",    mem_enabled      = True,)To learn more, see the PR and the Python SDK docs.Find memory leaks and heap growth: memory profiling for RustIn addition to CPU profiling, the Pyroscope Rust SDK now supports memory profiling through the jemalloc allocator. It reports in-use memory, so you can see which code paths allocated the most live memory and track down heap growth and leaks.To learn more, see the PR, the Rust SDK docs, and the jemalloc example.Profile .NET applications on Windows If you run .NET applications on Windows, including .NET Framework applications hosted in IIS, you can now send profiles from them to Pyroscope and find hot spots without migrating them first. Windows support is for x64, starting with version 1.3.0 of the profiler. On .NET 8, 9, and 10, you get the same profile types on Windows as on Linux, enabled with the same environment variables. On .NET Framework 4.7 and later, CPU and wall-time profiling are available.To learn more, see the PR and the .NET SDK docs. Note: this feature is currently in public preview. Let AI agents work with your profiling dataWithout access to your profiles, an AI coding agent can only reason about why a service is slow from the code in front of it, or you have to copy flame graphs and numbers into the conversation by hand. With access to your profiles, it can work from the same data you would, with visibility into which services use the most resources, which functions are responsible, and what a specific profile looked like at a specific time.gcx, the Grafana CLI, gives you and your AI coding agent structured access to your Grafana instance, from dashboards and alerts to metrics, logs, traces, and profiles. gcx enables agent mode automatically in many coding agents, such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor, and you can enable it yourself for any other agent with --agent. gcx now also includes gcx profiles commands for querying Pyroscope. To see gcx in action with Pyroscope, both in the terminal and with an AI agent, watch this community call.Below are some of the ways you can use gcx with your profiling data, whether you run the commands yourself or an agent runs them for you. You don't need to run your own stack to try them. Grafana Play has demo data you can query
